questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: A hand lens helps you see small things closely.
questions.explanation: A hand lens makes small things look bigger. We use it to look closely at a leaf, an ant or a seed.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Match each tool to its job.
questions.explanation: A ruler measures length. A hand lens helps us look closely. A thermometer shows how hot or cold. A timer shows how long something takes.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Put the steps in order. What does a scientist do first? Then?
questions.explanation: A scientist asks a question, makes a guess, tests it, records what happens and then tells other people.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: To find which ball bounces highest, we drop every ball from the same height.
questions.explanation: Dropping every ball from the same height makes the test fair. Then only the ball is different.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: In a fair test, we keep things the ___.
questions.explanation: In a fair test we keep things the same. We only change one thing.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: How do young scientists stay safe? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: We listen to our teacher, wash our hands and ask before we smell anything. We never taste things in a test, and we do not run around.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Which tool would you use? Sort each job.
items: how tall a bean plant is
how long sand takes to fall
questions.explanation: A ruler measures length and height. A thermometer measures how hot or cold. A timer measures how long something takes.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Before the test, Mina says: 'I think the rubber ball will bounce highest.' What is this?
questions.explanation: A prediction is a good guess about what will happen. A result is what we see after the test.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Look at the thermometers. Which one shows the hottest?
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C. A is at 12 degrees, B at 37 degrees and C at 48 degrees.
questions.explanation: The red line goes highest on thermometer C. A higher line means hotter.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Which tool measures how long a book is?
questions.explanation: A ruler measures how long something is. The stopwatch is for time, the thermometer is for how hot, and the balance scale is for how heavy.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Sort the tools. Which ones measure? Which ones help you look closely?
questions.explanation: Rulers, thermometers and stopwatches give us numbers. Hand lenses and microscopes make tiny things easier to see.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Look at the thermometers. Put them in order from hottest to coldest.
questions.image_alt: Three thermometers A, B and C. A shows 5 degrees, B shows 25 degrees and C shows 40 degrees.
questions.explanation: The line is highest on C, so C is the hottest. B is in the middle. The line is lowest on A, so A is the coldest.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Nadia drew these pictures each week. The tadpoles grew into frogs.
questions.image_alt: Life cycle of a frog: eggs, tadpole, froglet, adult frog.
questions.explanation: Nadia looked closely and drew what she saw. The picture shows eggs, then tadpoles, then froglets, then adult frogs.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Which part of your body helps you see what a leaf looks like?
questions.explanation: We use our eyes to see. Looking closely is one way to find out about things.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Mina and Raju race toy cars down a ramp. Mina pushes her car. Raju lets his car go. Is it a fair test?
options: No. Mina pushed her car and Raju did not.
Yes. Both cars are on the same ramp.
Yes. Both children are in Class 1.
questions.explanation: Mina pushed, so her car got a head start. A fair race lets both cars go the same way.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Nadia sees tiny black wriggly things in the village pond. What does a young scientist do?
options: Guess a name and stop looking.
Look closely and draw what she sees.
questions.explanation: Scientists look closely and record what they see. We never taste things to find out, and one guess is not enough.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: At home, Joy finds a bottle of coloured liquid in the kitchen. He wants to know what it is. What is the safe choice?
options: Ask a grown-up and do not touch it.
questions.explanation: Some liquids are dangerous. We ask a grown-up and never smell, taste or touch things we do not know.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Tuli wants to know how tall her bean plant is. She measures it with a ___.
questions.explanation: A ruler measures how tall or how long something is.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Class 1 dropped three balls. Why did they drop every ball from the same height?
questions.model_answer: To make it a fair test. The height was the same for every ball.
questions.explanation: If one ball was dropped from higher up, we could not tell why it bounced higher. Keeping the height the same makes the test fair.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Match each science step to an example.
pairs: I think the big stone will sink.
questions.explanation: A question starts an investigation. A prediction is a guess before the test. We record what we see and then share it.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Class 1 dropped balls from the same height. Bounce in hand spans: rubber ball 6, tennis ball 4, football 3. The ___ bounced the lowest.
questions.explanation: The football has the smallest number, 3, so it bounced the lowest. The rubber ball bounced highest with 6.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Class 1 dropped balls from the same height. Bounce in hand spans: rubber ball 6, tennis ball 4, football 3. How much higher did the rubber ball bounce than the tennis ball?
questions.explanation: 6 take away 4 is 2. The rubber ball bounced 2 hand spans higher than the tennis ball.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Tuli tests two paper planes. She throws plane A very hard and plane B gently. Plane A flies further. What should she change?
options: Throw plane B even more gently.
Throw both planes in the same way.
questions.explanation: Tuli threw the planes differently, so we cannot tell if the plane or the throw made the difference. Throwing both the same way makes it fair.

questions.title: Young Scientists
questions.stem: Joy grows two bean plants in the same kind of pot. Plant A is in the sun and gets water. Plant B is in a dark cupboard and gets no water. Which things are different? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: The water and the light are different. Because two things changed, Joy cannot tell which one made plant B small. A fair test changes only one thing.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Which one is a living thing?
questions.explanation: A goat is alive. It eats, grows and has young. A stone, a bicycle and a chair are never alive.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Sort the pictures into living and non-living.
questions.explanation: Worms, flowers and goats grow, feed and have young, so they are living. A teddy bear, a bicycle and a stone are non-living.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Living things need food, air and ___ to stay alive.
questions.explanation: All living things need water. Food, water and air keep them alive.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: A mango tree is not alive because it cannot walk.
questions.explanation: A mango tree is alive. It grows, takes in water through its roots and makes seeds. Plants do not need to walk to be alive.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: A toy car is alive because it moves.
questions.explanation: A car can move, but it cannot grow, feed or have young. Things that only move are not alive.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: What do living things do? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Living things grow, have young and need food. Wheels and batteries belong to machines, not to living things.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Match each picture to what a living thing needs.
questions.explanation: Living things need food, water, light and warmth, and a safe place to live (shelter).

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Living things grow and change. Put these pictures in order from youngest to oldest.
questions.explanation: A person starts as a baby, grows into a child, then an adult, and later becomes an older person.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Which thing do all living things do?
questions.explanation: All living things grow. Not all of them talk or fly.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Raju's toy robot can move and make sounds. Is it alive?
options: No. It cannot grow, eat or have young.
questions.explanation: A robot can move and make sounds, but it does not grow, eat or have young. So it is not alive.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Sort these. Which ones do living things need?
questions.explanation: Living things need food, water, air and shelter to stay alive. They can live without toys, sweets or a television.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Class 1 watered one plate of bean seeds. They kept another plate dry. After one week, 9 seeds grew on the wet plate and ___ seeds grew on the dry plate.
questions.explanation: No seeds grew on the dry plate. The seeds needed water to start growing.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Arif finds a stone by the river. It rolled down the hill, so he thinks it is alive. Which question helps him most?
questions.explanation: Living things eat and grow. A stone has no food, never grows and cannot have babies. Water pushed it, so it only moved.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Sumi forgot to give her pot plant ___ for a week. Its leaves are drooping.
questions.explanation: Plants need water. Without it the leaves droop. Sumi should water her plant.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Imran keeps a pet goat. What must he give it? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: A goat needs food, water and a shelter to stay safe and warm. A toy car and a bicycle are things it does not need.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Joy has a small pot plant. Where should he put it so that it grows well?
questions.explanation: Plants need light and warmth to grow well. A sunny window sill gives them both.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Look at the four plants. What happens to a plant that has no water?
questions.image_alt: Four potted plants: one healthy, one wilted with no water, one pale with no light and one small because it is too cold.
questions.explanation: The plant with no water droops. The plant with no light turns pale. The plant that is too cold stays small.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Which pictures show living things? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: A cat, a butterfly and a rice plant are alive. They grow and need food. A chair and a bicycle are made by people and are never alive.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Look at the picture. A chick grows into a hen.
questions.image_alt: Life cycle of a chicken: egg, hatching, chick, adult hen.
questions.explanation: The picture shows an egg, then a chick, then an adult hen. Living things grow and change.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Mina tests if bean seeds need water. Which test is fair?
options: One plate wet on the window sill. One plate dry in a dark cupboard.
One plate wet on the window sill. One plate dry on the same window sill.
Both plates wet on the window sill.
questions.explanation: In a fair test only one thing changes. Both plates sit in the same place, and only the water is different. In the first test, the light changes too.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Look at this list: cat, chair, mango tree, stone, snail, bicycle. How many living things are in it?
questions.explanation: The cat, the mango tree and the snail are living. The chair, the stone and the bicycle are non-living. That makes 3.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Mina thinks a toy car is alive because it moves. Tell one thing a living thing does that a car cannot do.
questions.model_answer: A living thing can grow, eat or have young. A car cannot.
questions.explanation: Living things grow, eat, breathe and have young. A car cannot do any of these, so it is not alive.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to grow a bean plant.
sequence: Plant a bean seed in soil.
The shoot grows into a bean plant.
questions.explanation: A seed needs water to start growing. First a shoot comes up, then it grows into a plant.

questions.title: Living Things and What They Need
questions.stem: In the seed test, 9 seeds grew on the wet plate and 0 on the dry plate. What does the test show?
questions.explanation: Only the water was different between the plates, so the test shows that seeds need water. It did not test soil or music.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Match each animal to its home.
questions.explanation: A fish lives in water and a monkey lives in trees. An earthworm lives under the ground. A bird flies in the sky.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: An animal that lives in trees is…
questions.explanation: Arboreal means living in trees. Aquatic means living in water. Fossorial means living under the ground.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: A habitat is the ___ of a plant or an animal.
questions.explanation: A habitat is the home of a living thing. It gives food, water, air and shelter.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: A fish can live on dry land.
questions.explanation: A fish needs water to breathe and swim. Its habitat is a pond, a river or the sea.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Where does each animal live? Sort them.
questions.explanation: Fish and frogs live in water. Monkeys and parrots live in trees. Earthworms and rats dig and live under the ground.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Which animals are aquatic? They live in water. Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Crabs, frogs, ducks and fish all live in or near water. A cow lives on the land and a monkey lives in trees.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Put the homes in order from the highest to the lowest.
questions.explanation: Birds fly in the sky. Monkeys live in trees. Cows walk on the ground. Earthworms live under the ground.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: the home of a living thing
questions.explanation: These five words help us name where animals live.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: How does a pond help a frog?
options: Water to swim in and insects to eat.
Branches to climb and sleep on.
Soil to dig a tunnel in.
questions.explanation: A pond gives a frog water to swim in, insects to eat and plants to hide under. Climbing branches is what a monkey needs.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Birds, bats and butterflies live in the sky. This is the ___ habitat.
questions.explanation: Aerial means in the air and sky. Birds, bats and butterflies fly there.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: A habitat gives a living thing food, water, air and shelter.
questions.explanation: A good habitat meets all the needs of the plants and animals that live there.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Look at the pond. Which number is the frog?
questions.image_alt: A pond with the Sun, air and clouds, a duck, a fish, water, a rock, water plants and a frog, each with a number.
questions.explanation: Number 8 is the frog. Number 4 is the fish, 7 is the water plants and 2 is the air and clouds.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Look at the pond. Which numbers show animals? Choose all that are right.
questions.image_alt: A pond with the Sun, air and clouds, a duck, a fish, water, a rock, water plants and a frog, each with a number.
questions.explanation: Number 3 is a duck, 4 is a fish and 8 is a frog. Number 5 is water and 6 is a rock, so they are not animals.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Look at the Sundarbans tree. What are its roots standing in?
questions.image_alt: A mangrove tree with breathing roots and prop roots in salty mud.
questions.explanation: Mangrove trees in the Sundarbans grow in salty mud. Their roots stand in the mud and hold the tree up.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Tuli goes by boat in the haor in Sylhet. She sees many fish and ducks. What kind of habitat is this?
questions.explanation: A haor is a big wetland full of water. Fish and ducks live there, so it is an aquatic habitat.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Anika visits a pond with her class to count the animals. What is the safe way?
options: Reach into the water to catch them.
Look with her teacher and do not touch.
questions.explanation: We look, count and do not touch. Staying with a grown-up near water keeps us safe and does not harm the animals.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Moung wants to see an earthworm in the garden. Where should he look?
options: in the soil under a stone
questions.explanation: Earthworms live in the soil under the ground. They are fossorial animals.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: The Sundarbans has land, trees, water, holes in the mud and sky. It has every kind of habitat.
questions.explanation: Tigers and deer walk on land. Monkeys climb trees. Fish and crocodiles swim in the rivers. Crabs dig holes in the mud. Birds fly above.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Why can a fish not live in a tree?
questions.model_answer: A fish needs water to breathe and swim. A tree has no water.
questions.explanation: A fish needs water to breathe and swim. A tree is a habitat for monkeys and parrots, not for fish.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Crabs dig holes in the mud in the Sundarbans. A hole under the ground is a ___ habitat.
questions.explanation: Fossorial means living under the ground. Crabs, earthworms and rats use holes in the ground.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Anika sees a monkey eating fruit in a tree. What does the tree give the monkey? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: A tree gives a monkey fruit to eat, branches to climb and a place to sleep. A monkey does not swim or dig.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Class 1 counted animals in 5 minutes. Pond: 4 frogs and 6 fish. Garden: 9 ants and 3 butterflies. Which place had more animals?
questions.explanation: The pond had 4 + 6 = 10 animals. The garden had 9 + 3 = 12 animals. The garden had 2 more.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: A kingfisher sits on a branch by a pond. It flies over the water and dives in to catch a fish. Which habitats does it use? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: The kingfisher flies in the sky, rests in a tree and hunts in the pond. It does not live under the ground.

questions.title: Habitats of Bangladesh
questions.stem: Ants walk on the land and dig homes in the soil. Which two words fit their habitats?
questions.explanation: Terrestrial means on land and fossorial means under the ground. An animal can live in more than one habitat.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Which food helps your body grow?
questions.explanation: An egg is a body-building food. It helps you grow. Fish, dal and milk help you grow too.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Which foods should we eat often? Which only a little?
questions.explanation: Rice, eggs and green vegetables give us energy, help us grow and keep us healthy. Sweets, chips and doughnuts are fine only as a small treat.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: A balanced diet has some of each kind of food and plenty of ___.
questions.explanation: We need to drink plenty of water every day, as well as eating different kinds of food.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Washing your hands with soap gets rid of germs.
questions.explanation: Soap and water wash germs off your hands. Clean hands help stop you getting ill.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: A fizzy drink is the best drink for a healthy body.
questions.explanation: Water is the best drink for your body. Fizzy drinks are full of sugar and do not help you grow.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: How can you keep your body healthy? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Exercise, clean hands and clean teeth keep us healthy. We also need plenty of sleep and many kinds of food, not only sweets.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Match each picture to what it does for your body.
questions.explanation: Rice and roti give us energy. Fish, egg and dal help us grow. Fruit and vegetables protect us. We also drink plenty of water.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Children need to sleep about ___ hours every night.
questions.explanation: Children need about 10 hours of sleep. Sleep rests the body and helps us feel good the next day.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Put the steps for washing hands in order.
questions.explanation: Wet your hands first, then use soap and rub for 20 seconds. Rinse the soap away and dry your hands last.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Which meal is the most balanced?
options: chips, a sweet cake and a fizzy drink
questions.explanation: Rice gives energy, fish helps us grow, spinach keeps us healthy, and water is the best drink. The other meals have no body-building or protecting foods.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Rice and roti give us ___.
questions.explanation: Rice, roti and potato are energy foods. They give us the energy to play and learn.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Class 1 put pretend germs (glitter) on their hands, then washed. Spots left: water 5 seconds, 30. Water 20 seconds, 15. Soap 20 seconds, 2. Which way cleaned best?
questions.explanation: Fewer spots mean cleaner hands. Soap for 20 seconds left only 2 spots, so it cleaned best.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Which food helps protect your body and keeps you healthy?
questions.explanation: Green vegetables and fruit have vitamins and fibre. They protect us and keep us healthy.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Which pictures show healthy habits? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Washing with soap, running and brushing your teeth keep you healthy. Sweets and doughnuts are only for a small treat.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Match each picture to why it helps.
questions.explanation: Soap removes germs, brushing cleans teeth, sleep rests the body and running makes muscles strong.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Rafi's lunch is chips, a sweet cake and a fizzy drink. What should he change?
options: Drink water and add a banana.
questions.explanation: Water is a better drink, and a banana is a protecting food. Rafi also needs foods that help him grow, such as rice, dal or fish.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Tumpa watched cartoons until late. At school she is sleepy. What should she do tonight?
questions.explanation: Her body needs sleep. Going to bed early helps her feel awake and ready to play at school.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Mina has been playing football in the mud. Now it is time to eat lunch. What should she do first?
options: Wash her hands with soap and water.
Wipe her hands on her shirt.
questions.explanation: Muddy hands can carry germs. Washing with soap and water before eating helps keep us well.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Anika feels grumpy after a long day. Resting or playing with friends can help her feel better.
questions.explanation: Rest and fun help our bodies and our feelings. Playing with friends and relaxing keep us happy and well.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Anika wants to be active every day. What can she do? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Walking, playing cricket and skipping make our bodies move and grow strong. Sitting or lying down all day does not.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Tumpa feels tired at school. Give her one tip to feel better.
questions.model_answer: Go to bed early, or eat a good breakfast, or play outside.
questions.explanation: A tired body needs sleep, good food and exercise. Any of these tips can help Tumpa feel better.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Nadia's dinner is rice, roti and potato. What should she add to make it balanced?
questions.explanation: Rice, roti and potato are all energy foods. Fish helps her grow and spinach protects her, so she needs both.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: In the glitter test, water for 5 seconds left 30 spots. Soap for 20 seconds left 2 spots. How many fewer spots did soap for 20 seconds leave?
questions.explanation: 30 take away 2 is 28. Soap for 20 seconds took away 28 more spots than water for 5 seconds.

questions.title: Healthy Bodies
questions.stem: Water for 5 seconds left 30 glitter spots. Soap for 20 seconds left 2 spots. Sumi says: 'They clean just as well.' Is Sumi right?
questions.explanation: 30 spots is much more than 2 spots. Soap and 20 seconds cleaned much better than a quick rinse.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Look at the stick and its shadow. When is the shadow shortest?
questions.image_alt: A stick and its shadow in the morning, at midday and in the evening as the Sun moves across the sky.
questions.explanation: At midday the Sun is high in the sky, so the shadow is short. In the morning and evening the Sun is low and the shadow is long.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Look at the picture. The stick's shadow is long in the morning and in the evening.
questions.image_alt: A stick and its shadow in the morning, at midday and in the evening as the Sun moves across the sky.
questions.explanation: When the Sun is low in the sky, shadows are long. This happens in the morning and the evening.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Look at the spinning Earth. The side facing the Sun has day.
questions.image_alt: The Sun lights one half of the spinning Earth: day on the side facing the Sun, night on the other side.
questions.explanation: The side of the Earth facing the Sun has day. The side facing away from the Sun has night.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Look at the Moon's shapes. Which number is the full Moon?
questions.image_alt: Eight shapes of the Moon numbered 1 to 8. Number 1 is the new Moon and number 5 is the full Moon.
questions.explanation: Number 5 is the full Moon, round and bright. Number 1 is the new Moon, when we can hardly see it.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: What do we see in the sky by day? What do we see by night?
questions.explanation: We see the Sun, sunrise and rainbows in the day. Stars are in the sky all the time, but we can only see them at night.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: The Sun rises in the ___ and sets in the west.
questions.explanation: Every morning the Sun comes up in the east. In the evening it goes down in the west.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: The Earth ___, so we have day and night.
questions.explanation: The Earth spins round. The side facing the Sun has day and the side facing away has night.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: The Moon makes its own light.
questions.explanation: The Moon does not make light. It shines because it reflects light from the Sun.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Shadows are shortest at midday.
questions.explanation: At midday the Sun is highest in the sky, so shadows are short.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Put these in order, from morning to night.
sequence: The Sun rises in the east.
The Sun is high at midday.
The Sun sets in the west.
questions.explanation: The Sun seems to climb up in the morning, is highest at midday and goes down in the evening. Then we see the stars.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Mina shines a torch on a ball in a dark room. The torch stands for the…
questions.explanation: The torch is the Sun and the ball is the Earth. The lit side of the ball has day and the dark side has night.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.subskill: Sun and Moon in our culture
questions.stem: Match each one to what it means.
questions.explanation: The Sun and Moon matter to many people. Muslims break their fast at sunset in Ramadan. Eid begins when the new Moon is seen. Pohela Boishakh welcomes the new Bangla year.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: What is true about the Sun? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: The Sun rises in the east, is highest at midday and sets in the west. It does not go out at night. The Earth spins so our side faces away from it.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Match each picture to what it shows.
questions.explanation: At sunrise the Sun comes up. At night we see stars. A full Moon looks round and bright. The Sun gives us light and heat.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Raju wants to see the Sun. What is the safe way?
options: Look straight at it for a short time.
Look at the shadow it makes instead.
questions.explanation: Never look straight at the Sun. It can hurt your eyes. We can watch the shadows instead.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.subskill: Sun and Moon in our culture
questions.stem: On the last evening of Ramadan, Imran's family looks for the new Moon. Where should they look?
questions.explanation: A thin new Moon is low in the western sky just after sunset. When the family sees it, they know Eid will start the next day.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: At 12 o'clock Tuli plays outside. Her shadow is very short. Why?
options: The Sun is high in the sky.
questions.explanation: At midday the Sun is high in the sky, so shadows are short.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Class 1 measured a stick's shadow. At 9 o'clock it was 6 hand spans. At 12 o'clock it was 1 hand span. At 3 o'clock it was 5 hand spans. The shadow was shortest at ___ o'clock.
questions.explanation: 1 hand span is the smallest number, so the shadow was shortest at 12 o'clock. The Sun is highest at midday.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: It is daytime for Nadia in Dhaka. Her uncle in another country says it is dark there. This can happen because the Earth spins.
questions.explanation: The Earth spins, so when one side faces the Sun, the other side faces away. It can be day in one country and night in another.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Why do we have day and night?
questions.model_answer: The Earth spins. The side facing the Sun has day and the side facing away has night.
questions.explanation: The Sun does not really move. The Earth spins, so each side takes a turn facing the Sun.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Look at the picture. The object blocks the ___, so there is a shadow.
questions.image_alt: A torch shines on an object and the object's shadow falls on a screen.
questions.explanation: A shadow forms behind an object when the object blocks the light from the torch or the Sun.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Mina measured a shadow. 9 o'clock: 6 hand spans. 12 o'clock: 1 hand span. 3 o'clock: 5 hand spans. When was the Sun highest in the sky?
questions.explanation: The shortest shadow means the Sun is highest. The shadow was shortest at 12 o'clock.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Look at the picture. In the morning the shadow points to the west. Where is the Sun in the morning?
questions.image_alt: A stick and its shadow in the morning, at midday and in the evening. The morning shadow points west and the evening shadow points east.
questions.explanation: A shadow falls on the opposite side to the Sun. The shadow points west, so the Sun is in the east. That is where the Sun rises.

questions.title: The Sun, Moon and Stars
questions.stem: Rafi says: 'It is night because the Sun goes out.' Which idea is right?
options: The Earth spins, so our side turns away from the Sun.
The Sun goes to sleep at night.
questions.explanation: The Sun does not go out. The Earth spins, so at night our side faces away from the Sun.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Match each kind of weather to what you wear or use.
questions.explanation: An umbrella keeps us dry in the rain. A sun hat keeps the Sun off our head. A scarf and jumper keep us warm on a cold day.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Look at the weather tools. Which letter is the rain gauge?
questions.image_alt: Five weather tools lettered A to E: a thermometer, a rain gauge, a wind vane, an anemometer and a barometer.
questions.explanation: B is the rain gauge. It collects rain so we can see how much fell. A is the thermometer, which shows how hot it is.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Which picture shows windy weather?
questions.explanation: The wind picture shows air moving. Windy weather moves leaves, flags and kites.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Which weather tool would you use? Sort each job.
items: how full the rain bottle is
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures how hot or cold. A rain gauge collects rain. A wind flag points the way the wind blows.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: The monsoon brings good things and problems. Sort them.
questions.explanation: Monsoon rain gives rice fields water and turns the land green. Too much rain can make the rivers overflow and cause floods.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: We measure how hot it is with a ___. We measure rain with a rain ___.
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures how hot or cold it is. A rain gauge measures how much rain falls.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: The weather is the same every day.
questions.explanation: The weather changes from day to day. One day can be sunny and the next day can be rainy.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: A weather forecast tells us what the weather will be like.
questions.explanation: Forecasters use patterns in the weather to say what tomorrow will be like.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: In Bangladesh, the wet rainy season is called the…
questions.explanation: The wet season is the monsoon. It brings heavy rain, and rivers fill up.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: The seasons come round every year. Start with hot summer. What comes next?
questions.explanation: In Bangladesh the weather follows a pattern: hot summer, then the wet rainy season, then cool winter. Then the pattern starts again.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Which pictures show wet weather? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Rain clouds, storm clouds and an umbrella in the rain all show wet weather. The Sun and the wind are dry.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Match each weather word to its meaning.
pairs: what the air outside is like
a time of year with its own weather
telling what the weather will be
questions.explanation: Weather is what the air outside is like each day. A season is a time of year with its own weather. A forecast says what the weather will be.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Class 1 looked at the sky for 10 days. Sunny: 5 days. Cloudy: 3 days. Rainy: 2 days. The most common weather was ___.
questions.explanation: Sunny has the biggest number, 5 days. So sunny was the most common weather.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Look at the water cycle. Which number shows rain falling?
questions.image_alt: The water cycle with five stages numbered 1 to 5. Number 3 shows rain falling from a cloud.
questions.explanation: Number 3 is rain falling from the cloud. Rain gives us water for rivers, ponds and rice fields.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Water goes round and round. Put the journey of the water in order.
sequence: The Sun warms the river water.
The water rises into the air.
questions.explanation: The Sun warms water so it rises into the air and makes clouds. The rain falls and runs back into the rivers. Then the journey starts again.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Raju is flying his kite. Dark clouds come and thunder rumbles. What should he do?
questions.explanation: In a storm we go indoors. A kite or a tall tree can be dangerous in thunder and lightning.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Mina plays outside on a hot sunny day. What should she do? Choose all that are right.
options: Stay in the Sun all day.
questions.explanation: A hat, water and shade keep us cool on a hot day. A thick jumper makes us hotter, and staying in the Sun all day is not safe.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Why do farmers like the monsoon rain?
options: It makes the soil very dry.
It stops the rice seeds growing.
questions.explanation: Rice grows best in fields full of water. The monsoon rain fills the fields so farmers can plant rice.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: The radio says heavy rain is coming and the river may flood. What should Sumi's family do?
options: Go to play in the river water.
Stay outside and ignore the news.
Move to a higher, safe place.
questions.explanation: A forecast helps us get ready. Moving to a higher, safe place keeps the family away from the flood water.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Tuli empties her rain gauge every evening. Today it holds more water than yesterday. This means more rain fell today.
questions.explanation: A rain gauge collects the rain that falls. More water in the gauge means more rain fell.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Look at the weather tools. Which letter shows which way the wind blows?
questions.image_alt: Five weather tools lettered A to E: a thermometer, a rain gauge, a wind vane that points the way the wind blows, an anemometer and a barometer.
questions.explanation: C is the wind vane. It turns and points the way the wind is blowing, like a wind flag.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Class 1 looked at the sky for 10 days. Sunny: 5 days. Cloudy: 3 days. Rainy: 2 days. On how many days was it cloudy or rainy?
questions.explanation: 3 cloudy days plus 2 rainy days is 5 days.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Class 1 saw sunny weather on 5 of 10 days. Raju says: 'It will be sunny tomorrow for sure.' Is Raju right?
questions.explanation: Patterns help us guess, but the weather can change. Tomorrow could be cloudy or rainy. A forecast is a good guess, not a sure thing.

questions.title: Weather Watching
questions.stem: Why do people listen to the weather forecast in the monsoon?
questions.model_answer: To know when heavy rain and floods may come, so they can stay safe.
questions.explanation: Too much rain can bring floods. The forecast tells people to get ready and stay safe.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Which picture shows something that harms the environment?
questions.explanation: Smoke makes the air dirty, so it harms the environment. Bins, trees and cloth bags help to keep it clean.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Which bin? Match each piece of waste to its bin.
questions.explanation: We sort waste by what it is made of. Paper, plastic and metal can be recycled. A mango peel is food waste, so it goes to compost.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Which pictures show a healthy environment? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Trees, clean water and litter in a bin all help keep the environment healthy. Oil in water and smoke harm it.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Does it help or harm the environment? Sort the pictures.
questions.explanation: Trees clean the air. A cloth bag can be used again and again, and a bin keeps litter off the ground. Oil and smoke make the water and air dirty.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Which picture shows reusing?
questions.explanation: We can use a cloth bag again and again. Reuse means to use something again.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: This banana skin is food waste. Where should it go?
questions.image_alt: A banana.
questions.explanation: Food waste rots and makes the soil rich. We put it in compost, not in the paper, metal or plastic bins.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Reduce, reuse or recycle? Sort each idea.
items: use both sides of the paper
take only the food you can eat
use an old jar as a pencil pot
carry a cloth bag again and again
put cans in the metal bin
put old paper in the paper bin
questions.explanation: Reduce means use less. Reuse means use again. Recycle means make something new from old things.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: The three Rs are reduce, reuse and ___.
questions.explanation: Reduce, reuse and recycle are the three Rs. They help us make less rubbish.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Food waste can be made into compost.
questions.explanation: Food waste rots and makes the soil rich. Gardeners use compost to help plants grow.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Cutting down lots of trees helps keep our air clean.
questions.explanation: Trees help keep the air clean and are homes for animals. Cutting down lots of trees harms the environment.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: What does a healthy environment have? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: A healthy environment has clean water, plenty of trees and fresh air. Litter and smoke make it unhealthy.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to sort the class rubbish.
sequence: Empty the bin onto a sheet.
questions.explanation: We wear gloves first to stay safe. Then we empty, sort and count the waste, and wash our hands at the end.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Reduce means to use less.
questions.explanation: To reduce is to use less. When we use less, we make less rubbish.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Class 1 sorted their bin. Paper: 12. Plastic: 8. Food: 5. Metal: 2. They had the most ___ waste.
questions.explanation: 12 is the biggest number, so there was most paper waste. They can use both sides of the paper to make less.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Match each harmful action to the problem it causes.
questions.explanation: Litter can hurt animals, and smoke makes the air dirty. Dirty water can make people ill. Trees are homes for animals.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Moung sees a broken glass bottle on the playground. What should he do?
options: Pick it up with his hands.
questions.explanation: Broken glass can cut us. We never touch it. We tell a teacher so a grown-up can clear it safely.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Plastic bags blow around Tuli's playground. What is a good plan?
options: Put labelled bins in each class.
Burn all the bags behind the school.
Throw the bags into the pond.
questions.explanation: Bins in every class help children put litter in the right place. Burning bags makes smoke, and bags in a pond harm the water and animals.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: After cooking, Anika's family has fruit peels and vegetable scraps. What can they do?
questions.explanation: Peels and scraps rot and make rich compost for plants. Burning and throwing them in the river harm the air and the water.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: At the market, Nadia takes her own cloth bag instead of a new plastic bag each time. This helps the environment.
questions.explanation: Using a cloth bag again and again means less plastic is thrown away. This is reusing.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: How can our school stay clean and healthy? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Bins, trees and clean toilets keep a school healthy. Litter makes the playground dirty, and running taps waste water.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Write one thing you can do to keep your school clean.
questions.model_answer: I can put my litter in the bin.
questions.explanation: Putting litter in the bin, sorting waste and planting trees all help keep a school clean and healthy.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Class 1 sorted their bin. Paper: 12. Plastic: 8. Food: 5. Metal: 2. How many pieces of waste were there in all?
questions.explanation: 12 + 8 = 20. 20 + 5 = 25. 25 + 2 = 27. There were 27 pieces of waste.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Class 1 had 12 pieces of paper, 8 of plastic, 5 of food and 2 of metal. They want to make less rubbish. What is the best first plan?
options: Use both sides of the paper.
Use fewer metal tins in class.
questions.explanation: Paper was the biggest pile. Using both sides of the paper makes the biggest change.

questions.title: Keeping Our Environment Clean
questions.stem: Class 1 found 12 pieces of paper, 5 of food and 2 of metal. Food and metal together are how many fewer than paper?
questions.explanation: Food and metal together are 5 + 2 = 7. Paper is 12. 12 take away 7 is 5, so food and metal together are 5 fewer.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Which picture shows a natural material?
questions.explanation: Wood comes from trees, so it is natural. Plastic and glass are made by people.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Natural or made by people? Sort the pictures.
questions.explanation: Wood, stone and wool come from nature. Plastic, glass and paper are made by people.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Wool is a natural material.
questions.explanation: Wool comes from sheep, so it is natural.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Paper is found in nature. People do not make it.
questions.explanation: People make paper in factories or by hand. It is not found in nature.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: We can ___ a sponge by pressing it hard.
questions.explanation: Pressing hard on a sponge squashes it.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Match each action to the thing you do it to.
questions.explanation: We squash a sponge, stretch a rubber band, twist a wet towel and bend a pipe cleaner.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Which one can we stretch?
questions.explanation: A balloon stretches when we blow it up. A stone and a brick do not stretch.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Which goes back to its shape after squashing?
questions.explanation: A sponge goes back to its shape. Clay stays in its new shape.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Why is a ball made of rubber, not stone?
questions.model_answer: Rubber bounces and is soft. A stone is hard and would hurt.
questions.explanation: Rubber is soft and bounces. A stone is hard and does not bounce.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to make a clay pot.
sequence: Dig clay from the river bank.
Squash and shape the clay on the wheel.
Dry the pot in the sun.
Heat the pot in a hot kiln.
questions.explanation: Mr Paul digs the clay, shapes it on the wheel, dries the pot and then heats it in the kiln.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Mr Paul heats clay pots in a kiln. What happens?
questions.explanation: Heating in the kiln makes the clay hard. It will never go soft again.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Joy wants a toy he can squash and shape. Which is best?
questions.explanation: Clay is soft and can be squashed into new shapes. Stone and glass are hard.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Nadia twists a wet towel to dry it. This changes its shape.
questions.explanation: Twisting changes the shape of a towel and squeezes the water out.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Which are made by people? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Plastic, glass and paper are made by people. Stone and wool come from nature.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Match each picture to its material.
questions.explanation: A chair is made of wood, a key of metal and a bottle of plastic. Socks are made of cloth.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Which picture shows something made of metal?
questions.explanation: A key is made of metal. A newspaper is paper and a teddy bear is cloth.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: A sponge stays flat after you squash it and let go.
questions.explanation: A sponge goes back to its shape. Clay is the one that stays flat.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Squashing, bending, twisting and ___ change the shape of materials.
questions.explanation: The four ways to change shape are squashing, bending, twisting and stretching.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Class 1 test: thin band 14 cm, medium 11 cm, thick 8 cm. Which stretched most?
questions.explanation: The thin band became the longest, 14 cm, so it stretched the most.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Thin band: 14 cm. Thick band: 8 cm. How much longer is the thin band?
questions.explanation: 14 minus 8 is 6, so the thin band was 6 cm longer.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Rafi squashes clay and a sponge, then lets go. What happens?

options.text: The clay stays flat. The sponge springs back.
Both go back to their shape.

questions.explanation: Clay stays squashed. A sponge goes back to its shape.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Sort by what happens after you squash or stretch.
questions.explanation: A sponge and a rubber band go back to their shape. Clay, play dough and a bent pipe cleaner stay in the new shape.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Jute is a natural material.
questions.explanation: Jute comes from plants, so it is a natural material.

questions.title: Materials and Their Shapes
questions.stem: Which picture shows something made by people?
questions.explanation: A plastic bottle is made by people in a factory. Wood and stone come from nature.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Is it heating or cooling? Sort the changes.
questions.explanation: Ice melts, an egg cooks and water boils when they are heated. Water freezes, jelly sets and melted chocolate goes hard when they are cooled.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: An ice cube sits in the hot sun. What will it become?
questions.image_alt: An ice cube.
questions.explanation: Heat melts ice into water.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Which picture shows something that melts in the sun?
questions.explanation: Ice cream melts when it gets warm. A rock and a coin do not melt in the sun.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Which can melt when heated? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Ice, chocolate and ice cream melt when they are heated. A brick and a key do not melt in everyday heat.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Water boils and turns to steam.
questions.explanation: When water is heated until it boils, it turns into steam.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: This egg is cooked. It can turn back into a raw egg.
questions.image_alt: A fried egg in a pan.
questions.explanation: A cooked egg cannot go back. Cooking is a change that cannot go back.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Water turns into ice when it is ___.
questions.explanation: Cooling water makes it freeze into ice.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Salt ___ in water and seems to disappear.
questions.explanation: Salt dissolves in water. It mixes in and seems to disappear.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Melt is solid to liquid. Freeze is liquid to solid. Dissolve is mixing into water and seeming to disappear. Boil is water turning to steam.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to make pitha.
sequence: Mix rice flour and water into dough.
Steam the pitha over hot water.
The dough turns into a firm cake.
questions.explanation: Grandma mixes flour and water into dough. She steams it over hot water. The dough turns into a firm cake.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Mina leaves butter in the hot sun. What happens?
questions.explanation: Heat melts butter.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Rina wants ice cubes for a drink. Where should she put water?
questions.explanation: Cooling water makes it freeze. A freezer is very cold.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Imran stirs sugar in his tea. What happens to the sugar?
questions.explanation: Sugar dissolves in hot tea. It mixes in and seems to disappear.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Only grown-ups use the stove and hot water.
questions.explanation: Stoves and hot water can burn us. Children ask a grown-up for help.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Joy puts melted chocolate in the fridge. It goes hard again.
questions.explanation: Cooling makes melted chocolate go hard again. This change can go back.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Steam rises from a hot drink. When steam cools, it turns into...
questions.image_alt: A hot drink with steam.
questions.explanation: Steam turns back into water drops when it cools.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Match each picture to what happens.
questions.explanation: Ice melts when heated. A fried egg cooks and goes hard. Water drops freeze into ice when cooled.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Why does ice cream melt on a hot day?
questions.model_answer: The hot day heats the ice cream, so it melts into a liquid.
questions.explanation: Heat from the air and sun warms the ice cream. A solid ice cream turns into a liquid.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Which things dissolve in water? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Salt and sugar dissolve in water. Sand, rice and coins do not.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Can the change go back? Sort the changes.
questions.explanation: Ice melting, chocolate melting and water freezing can go back. A cooked egg and steamed pitha cannot.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Melting times: sun 10 minutes, classroom 25, fridge 60. Where did ice melt fastest?
questions.explanation: The shortest time was in the sun, 10 minutes, so ice melted fastest there.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Fridge: 60 minutes. Sun: 10 minutes. How many more minutes in the fridge?
questions.explanation: 60 minus 10 is 50, so the ice took 50 minutes longer in the fridge.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Is it a fair test to use ice cubes of different sizes?
questions.explanation: Big ice cubes take longer to melt. For a fair test the ice cubes must be the same size.

questions.title: Heating, Cooling and Dissolving
questions.stem: Sand dissolves in water.
questions.explanation: Sand does not dissolve. It sinks to the bottom.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Which are light sources? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: The Sun, a candle and a torch give out light. The Moon only reflects the Sun's light and a mirror reflects light.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Does it give out light? Sort the pictures.
questions.explanation: The Sun, a candle and a light bulb give out light. The Moon, a mirror and a book do not.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: The Moon is a light source.
questions.explanation: The Moon does not make light. It reflects light from the Sun.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: A shadow forms when light is blocked.
questions.explanation: When something blocks the light, a dark shadow forms behind it.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Sounds are made by vibrations.
questions.explanation: A vibration is a very fast shake. Every sound starts with one.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Darkness is when there is no ___.
questions.explanation: Darkness means there is no light, so we cannot see.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: To vibrate means to shake very ___.
questions.explanation: Vibrate means to shake very fast. A drum skin vibrates when you hit it.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Match each instrument to how we make its sound.
questions.explanation: We hit a drum, pluck the strings of a guitar and shake maracas. Each one vibrates to make sound.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Look at the picture. What blocks the light?
questions.image_alt: A torch, an object and its shadow on a screen.
questions.explanation: The object stops the light from the torch reaching the screen. The dark shape behind it is the shadow.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Which picture shows something that makes a sound?
questions.explanation: A bell makes a sound when it rings. A candle and a mirror do not make sound.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Which picture shows what we hear with?
questions.explanation: We hear sounds with our ears.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: The lights go out at night. What can Nadia use to see?
questions.explanation: A torch gives out light, so Nadia can see. A mirror and a radio do not make light.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Sumi holds a card between a lamp and the wall. What forms?
questions.explanation: The card blocks the light, so a dark shadow forms on the wall.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Imran plucks a rubber band. It makes a sound. Why?
questions.explanation: A plucked band shakes very fast. This vibration makes the sound.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Moung can see his toys in a completely dark room.
questions.explanation: We cannot see anything when there is no light.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Put the steps in order for a shadow puppet show.
sequence: Hold a puppet between the lamp and the cloth.
A dark shadow forms on the cloth.
questions.explanation: The lamp gives light. The puppet blocks the light. Then a dark shadow forms on the cloth.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Why does a drum make a sound when you hit it?
questions.model_answer: The drum skin vibrates (shakes very fast) when you hit it.
questions.explanation: Hitting the drum makes the drum skin shake very fast. This vibration makes the sound.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Toy far: shadow 8 cm. Middle: 14 cm. Near: 25 cm. What happens as it gets nearer?
questions.explanation: The shadow grows from 8 cm to 25 cm as the toy gets nearer the torch.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Near shadow: 25 cm. Far shadow: 8 cm. How much bigger is the near one?
questions.explanation: 25 minus 8 is 17, so the near shadow is 17 cm bigger.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Lina says the Moon is bright, so it makes light. Is she right?

options.text: Yes, the Moon is a big lamp.
Yes, it makes light like a star.

questions.explanation: The Moon only looks bright because it reflects light from the Sun. It is not a light source.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: Which make sounds? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: A drum, a loudspeaker and a barking dog all make sounds. A rock and a candle do not.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: We need light to see things.
questions.explanation: Without light we cannot see anything.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: What is the biggest light source for Earth?
questions.explanation: The Sun is the biggest light source. It lights up the day.

questions.title: Light and Sound
questions.stem: A shadow has the same shape as the thing blocking the light.
questions.explanation: A shadow has the shape of the object that blocks the light.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: The lamp in this circuit will light.
questions.image_alt: A circuit with a cell, a lamp and a closed switch.
questions.explanation: The loop is complete and the switch is closed, so electricity flows round and the lamp lights.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Why is the lamp off in this circuit?
questions.image_alt: A circuit with a cell, a lamp and an open switch.
questions.explanation: The open switch makes a gap in the loop. Electricity cannot flow round, so the lamp stays off.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Match each part of a circuit to its job.
questions.explanation: A cell pushes electricity round. A wire carries it. A switch turns the circuit on and off. A lamp gives light.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Is it safe or not safe? Sort the actions.
items: asking an adult to plug in
touching a switch with wet hands
questions.explanation: We use torches with batteries and ask an adult to plug things in. We never touch switches with wet hands or poke sockets.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Does it use electricity? Sort the pictures.
questions.explanation: A fan, a television and a mobile phone use electricity. A ball, a chair and a teddy bear do not.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: A circuit is a loop.
questions.explanation: A circuit is a complete loop. Electricity flows round it from the cell, through the lamp and back.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Electricity from the wall is safe to touch.
questions.explanation: Electricity from the wall is dangerous. Never touch sockets or wires.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: A switch can make a gap in a circuit.
questions.explanation: Opening a switch makes a gap, so the circuit is off. Closing it fills the gap.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: A lamp lights when the circuit is ___.
questions.explanation: Electricity can only flow round a complete circuit with no gaps.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: A cell is a battery that stores ___.
questions.explanation: A cell stores electricity and pushes it round the circuit.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Put the steps in order to make a lamp light.
sequence: Join the cell, wires and lamp in a loop.
questions.explanation: Join the parts in a loop, check there are no gaps, close the switch and then the lamp lights.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Which part turns a circuit on and off?
questions.explanation: A switch opens and closes the circuit. A lamp gives light and a wire carries electricity.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Which picture shows where solar electricity comes from?
questions.explanation: A solar panel turns sunlight into electricity.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Where does electricity come from? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Sunlight, wind and moving water can all make electricity. A stone and a teddy bear cannot.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: There are no wires on Shuvo's char. Where does his electricity come from?
questions.explanation: Shuvo's family has a solar panel on the roof. It turns sunlight into electricity.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Anika's hands are wet. A switch is on the wall. What should she do?
questions.explanation: Wet hands and electricity are dangerous. Anika asks an adult for help.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Mina's toy light does not work. A wire has fallen off the cell. Why?
questions.explanation: The wire is part of the loop. With a wire off, there is a gap and electricity cannot flow.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: At night, Shuvo's battery lights the lamps.
questions.explanation: The solar panel charges the battery in the day. At night the battery lights the lamps.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Why is a solar panel useful on the char?
questions.model_answer: There are no electricity wires on the char, so the solar panel makes electricity from sunlight.
questions.explanation: There are no electricity wires on the char. A solar panel makes electricity from sunlight.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: What happens to the bulb in a complete loop?

sim.task: Open Circuit Construction Kit: DC. Drag a battery, a light bulb and wires onto the board. Join them in one complete loop with no gaps. Watch the bulb.

questions.explanation: A bulb lights only when the loop is complete. Electricity flows from the battery through the bulb and back.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: The bulb stays lit when the switch is open.

sim.task: Open Circuit Construction Kit: DC. Make a loop with a battery, a bulb and wires, and add a switch. Click the switch to open it, then click it again to close it. Watch the bulb each time.

questions.explanation: An open switch makes a gap in the loop, so the bulb goes out. Closing the switch lights it again.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: A wire is off the loop. You close the switch. Does the lamp light?

options.text: No, it still has a gap.

questions.explanation: The missing wire leaves a gap, so closing the switch does not help.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Each torch uses 2 cells. How many cells do 3 torches need?
questions.explanation: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, so 3 torches need 6 cells.

questions.title: Electricity
questions.stem: Metal things such as a coin let electricity pass through.
questions.explanation: Metals let electricity through. Things like a rubber eraser do not.
